title: Incident summary for executives
prompt:
Summarize this incident for a non-technical executive audience in at most 80 words. Cover what happened, the customer impact, the fix, and one follow-up action.

Timeline (UTC):
09:14 Deploy of checkout-api v412 begins in the EU region.
09:16 Error rate on EU checkout rises to 100%. v412 reads a config key that was never set in EU.
09:31 On-call engineer paged by a customer-support escalation; the automated alert had been muted during last week's migration and never re-enabled.
09:43 Rollback to v411 completes. Error rate returns to normal.
Impact: 27 minutes of failed EU checkouts, about 1,900 failed orders. US and APAC unaffected.
system:
You are completing one task from an evaluation suite. Do the task as asked.

Reply with the requested text only, with no preamble about what you are doing.

rubric.name: cause
rubric.description: States the cause in plain language: a release needed a setting that was missing in the EU. No version numbers or config jargon required.

rubric.name: impact
rubric.description: States the impact with the facts given: EU checkout only, about 27 minutes, about 1,900 failed orders. Does not invent or alter numbers.

rubric.name: fix_and_follow_up
rubric.description: Says service was restored by rolling back, and names one concrete follow-up (for example re-enabling the muted alert).

rubric.name: audience_and_length
rubric.description: At most 80 words, and readable by a non-technical executive: no UTC timestamps, version numbers, or unexplained jargon.

reference:
A faulty release broke checkout for all EU customers for 27 minutes,
causing about 1,900 failed orders. Other regions were not affected. The release depended
on a setting that was missing in the EU. We restored service by rolling back to the
previous version. Our automatic alert had been switched off, which delayed the response,
so we are re-enabling it and adding a check that blocks releases when a required setting
is missing.
answers:
At 09:14 UTC the deploy of checkout-api v412 started and by 09:16 the error rate hit 100%
because v412 reads a config key that was never set. The on-call engineer got paged at
09:31 and rolled back to v411 at 09:43. This was a significant outage for the business and
we take it very seriously. Going forward the team will be more careful with deploys and
config keys, and we will look at improving our processes, tooling, culture and
communication across all regions so that this kind of thing is less likely to happen again
in the future.
